source.title: Steering Without Side Effects: Improving Post-Deployment Control of Language Models
source.authors: Asa Cooper Stickland; Alexander Lyzhov; Jacob Pfau; Salsabila Mahdi; Samuel R. Bowman

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper adds contrastive activation vectors and evaluates harmful-request compliance and general capability, but its vectors are derived from contrasting responses rather than harmful-versus-harmless instructions, and it does not perform the claimed ablation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports activation-addition results for jailbreak and prefill attack success, and for MT-Bench capability. It does not test whether adding the direction makes the model refuse harmless requests, or whether ablating a direction removes refusal. Hyperparameter-selection results and findings cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper adds a harmlessness steering vector as a tool and mainly reports how its KL-then-steer (KTS) method trades jailbreak success against MT-Bench. The vector contrasts refusing and complying responses (Bai et al. data), not harmful and harmless instructions. The paper never ablates it and never measures refusal induced on harmless prompts. Arditi et al. is cited only as concurrent work. The jailbreak and prefill ASR changes are a related steering effect, not a test of whether a single difference-in-means direction mediates refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors also report that KTS transfers to anti-sycophancy steering on TruthfulQA, and that probe or Llama Guard classifiers allow selective steering. The headline 44% jailbreak reduction comes from KTS combined with LoRA DPO, not from steering alone.
record.recipe_differences: Uses layer-specific mean differences between hidden states of good and bad responses to construct vectors, then adds them at layers 2–22 and every token position. It does not derive the direction from harmful versus harmless instructions or project a direction out.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering multiplier changes the trade-off between attack success and MT-Bench score; KTS training improves the capability scores at comparable steering strengths.

fits_no_version.finding: On Llama-2-7b-chat, adding a response-contrast harmlessness vector at layers 2-22 cuts jailbreak ASR only slightly (20.3 to 17.6) and prefill ASR more (92 to 74) at k=-0.75. MT-Bench falls from 6.53 to 4.67; KTS training softens this to 5.17.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation addition of a refusal-vs-compliance response vector modestly increases robustness to jailbreaks, at a capability cost that grows with steering strength.

record.problems: The evaluation uses one model family/checkpoint, and no uncertainty estimates are stated. The attack-success and capability results show a trade-off rather than refusal removal; the paper does not directly measure refusal on harmless prompts or test ablation.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted steering results for DPO LoRA combinations and system-prompt conditions, as well as classifier-conditioned steering, because these are additional comparison or control configurations beyond the main original-model and KTS steering results recorded here. Table 1 and Tables 5–6 report those results.

untested.parts: Direction from harmful vs harmless instructions; ablation removing refusal; addition inducing refusal on harmless prompts; single-direction mediation.
All parts; jailbreak mechanism not analysed, and no training against ablation.
All parts; KTS fine-tuning targets steering side-effects, not whether a removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification and V1 labels are rejected. The vector, the measure (ASR rather than refusal rate) and the focus (own-method side-effects) do not match V1. The text says the prefill baseline is 90%, while Table 1 gives 92% for the original model.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction, establish that one shared direction mediates refusal, or measure refusals on harmless requests.
Does not test whether jailbreak attacks work by suppressing the direction, or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
Does not compare one direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple directions.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
No cross-language, cross-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test.
KTS training is used to reduce steering side effects, but the paper does not test whether refusal-training history determines whether a removable direction exists.

relation.reason: It uses a refusal-like steering vector as a means to mitigate jailbreaks and tests only whether KTS reduces steering side effects. It does not test whether a single difference-in-means direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: The study builds a vector from good (refusing) minus bad (complying) responses to Bai et al. requests, following Zou et al. 2023a, and adds it as a tool. It reports KTS Pareto results (jailbreak/prefill ASR vs MT-Bench). It never builds the harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction, never ablates, and cites Arditi et al. only as concurrent work.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match Table 1. Caveats: Sec. 3.1 defines v = mean(good) − mean(bad) and Fig. 1 says 'Apply +vsteer', yet Table 1 lowers ASR with negative k, so the sign convention is unclear. Rows R13–R20 are the study's own KTS method. The authors_conclusion paraphrase checks out: the conclusion credits the 44% reduction to KTS combined with LoRA DPO.
